Follow live updates here. Healey to announce inflation-busting minimum wage rise
 Szu Ping Chan Mon, October 26, 2026 at 2:10 PM EDT 5 min read John Healey, pictured preparing his Budget in Downing Street, is expected to slow increases in the youth rates of the minimum wage - Treasury/Kirsty O'Connor John Healey will announce an inflation-busting increase in the minimum wage in the Budget. 
 The Chancellor is expected to increase the National Living Wage by just under 4pc on Wednesday, taking it above £13 an hour for the first time. 
 The size of the rise would outstrip inflation, which is currently running at 3.5pc and is expected to average around 3pc in 2027. 
 It represents a fresh headache for businesses already struggling to cope with rapidly rising wages, energy costs and taxes. 
 However, Mr Healey is also expected to slow increases in the youth rates of minimum wage, following a series of sharp rises under both Labour and the Conservatives. 
 Labour pledged to scrap the youth rates in its manifesto by raising them faster than the adult rate. However, employers have said that recent increases relative to the headline rate have made it unattractive to offer young people jobs. 
 Louise Hellem, the chief economist at the Confederation of British Industry, said: "The steep rises in employment costs over the last few years have made firms more cautious about hiring and reduced their ability to invest. 
 "This has had a significant impact on firms' ability to create entry-level roles, making it increasingly difficult for young people to take that crucial first step on the career ladder." 
 The decision to pull back, first reported by The Times, comes amid growing concern over the state of the jobs market for young people, with almost a million neither earning nor learning in Britain. 
 While employers will welcome the slowdown for the youth rate of minimum wage, bosses said an inflation-busting increase to the headline would still be challenging. 
 The move would deal another blow to the hospitality sector, which has around 330,000 jobs paid at or around the minimum wage and often provides young people with their first foothold in the jobs market. 
 Allen Simpson, the chief executive of UKHospitality, said: "Getting young people into work is a moral imperative for the whole of society. If the Government are slowing the minimum wage increase for young people, that will help, but we still desperately need a reverse of the NICs jobs tax which has made early career roles unaffordable." 
 Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, accused Labour of causing "a youth jobs emergency" and said: "Pushing the minimum wage up faster than inflation will cost more jobs and feed into family bills." 
 The Low Pay Commission (LPC), which advises the Government on minimum wage rates, said in March that it was minded to recommend an increase in the headline rate of minimum wage of up to 5pc. 
 Story Continues That was the top end of a range but its central estimate of around 3.7pc would still represent an above-inflation rise, taking minimum wage to £13.18 an hour from next April. 
 The 2026 Budget cover. The Chancellor will reveal its contents in the Commons on Wednesday - Treasury/Kirsty O'Connor Official earnings data published by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) last week, which are used by the LPC to calculate the minimum wage, raised the prospect of a bigger increase. 
 On Monday, Deutsche Bank forecast a 4.6pc rise based on the new data, while Morgan Stanley warned the increase could be as much as 5.5pc. 
 One figure involved in the discussions said the increases would be "inflation-tickling rather than inflation-busting", in a move designed to avoid alarming businesses. 
 However, Alex Hall-Chen, at the Institute of Directors (IoD), said businesses were still struggling to absorb the impact of Rachel Reeves's £25bn increase in employers' National Insurance contributions and the Employment Rights Act. 
 She said: "Combined with an increase in the National Living Wage of over 40pc since 2021, there is a crisis in the cost of employment which is leading many employers to curb hiring and look to automation and outsourcing as alternatives." 
 Raising the minimum wage faster than inflation could also potentially make it harder for the Bank of England to bring price rises under control. 
 James Smith, an economist at ING, said the minimum wage decision would be a key factor for the Bank of England next year. 
 He said: "If the Low Pay Commission says it should be much closer to 5pc, say – which I think would be a surprise – could the Government realistically say no to that? Probably not. For markets, that would really add to bets on rate hikes." 
 In a consultation published this spring, the LPC said its recommendations would take into account the state of the economy, the jobs market and living costs. 
 Mr Healey will also use the Budget to announce a series of smaller measures designed to ease cost of living pressures. 
 The Chancellor will confirm plans to scrap tariffs on imports of more than 100 products, including baked beans, cough sweets, chocolate and oat milk, which the Treasury said would save shoppers up to £185m a year. 
 He will also make a tax break for self-employed drivers permanent, extend parental pay to self-employed fathers and others who have been left out, and reform Carer's Allowance so that unpaid carers no longer lose their entire benefit when they exceed the earnings limit. 
 The Treasury declined to comment.
